title: True words aren't pretty
hook: true words aren't beautiful; the more the sage gives, the more he has (Tao Te Ching 81)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the small village: a country where people find their own food sweet and hear the neighbors' dogs. Your line was content at home.

Two notes after a job interview. One is from a recruiter: wonderful energy, so impressive, we'll be in touch. The other is from an old friend who looked at your answers: the second one rambled, and you never said why you want the job. One is lovely to read. The other is the one you'll actually use. Chapter eighty-one of the Tao Te Ching opens with that difference, and then, almost in the same breath, it turns to giving.
screen: `A LOVELY NOTE.` → `A USEFUL NOTE.` → `WHICH ONE IS TRUE?`

segments.voice: First, the opening pair. Words that are true aren't pretty, the chapter says, and pretty words aren't true. It's a mirror line: turn it around and it still holds. That doesn't mean every kind word is a lie. It means polish isn't the same thing as truth, and sometimes the polish is there to cover something. Second, two more pairs in the same shape. The good don't argue, and those who argue aren't good. Those who really know aren't widely learned, and the widely learned don't really know. These sound harsh until you remember chapter seventy-one, where the best knowing was knowing you don't know. Piling up facts and winning debates are both set to one side. Third, the turn, where our line comes from. The sage doesn't hoard. The more the sage does for others, the more the sage has. The more the sage gives, the more the sage's own store grows. As arithmetic, it's nonsense. As a life, it starts to make sense: a teacher who explains a thing understands it better; a cook who feeds people gets a full table. Fourth, the closing lines. Heaven's way is to benefit and not harm. The sage's way is to act and not contend. After all the water, valleys and uncarved wood, the chapter settles on giving without fighting: the plain sentence instead of the shiny one, the thing handed over without a receipt.
screen: `TRUE WORDS AREN'T PRETTY.` · `THE ARGUER, THE PILED-UP LEARNING.` · `THE MORE HE GIVES, THE MORE HE HAS.` · `BENEFIT, DON'T HARM. ACT, DON'T FIGHT.` · then, large: `THE MORE I GIVE.`

segments.voice: Look around your life for one thing someone else could use: a coat in the closet, a finished book, an hour, a skill like fixing a bike or reading a lease, or a true word someone needs, said plainly and kindly. Pick one and picture handing it over. Then notice what's left in your own hands afterward.
True words aren't pretty. Chapter eighty-one: true words aren't beautiful, and beautiful words aren't true; the more the sage gives, the more the sage has. Today's word.
Your line: the more I give. A plain, true word counts as a gift, too. That's day one thousand one hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter eighty-one as a summary of the sage's way: speak plainly, don't argue for the sake of winning, don't hoard, and find that giving to others leaves you with more.

original.note: Chinese: true words aren't beautiful, the opening of chapter eighty-one.

trapdoor: what you thought: true words aren't pretty means honest people are blunt.
what it means: polish isn't truth; and giving, not hoarding, is how the sage's store grows.
what a scholar hears: the chapter is built from mirrored pairs, a shape the book uses elsewhere too, and it ends on 'act and don't contend', echoing earlier chapters on not fighting.
guess: honest words often lack polish, and polish can hide the truth
only harsh words can be trusted, so kindness is a lie
plain speech is rude, so the wise say very little at all

chat.says: How can giving things away leave you with more? That sounds backwards.
options: Not as arithmetic, as a life: explaining a thing helps you understand it better.
It's a promise that money you give away will come back to you, with extra.
It means the sage keeps careful count, so every gift gets paid back in time.
chat.meaning: Chapter eighty-one says the more the sage gives, the more the sage has. It makes sense as a life: a teacher who explains understands better.

Tao Te Ching.meaning: the short Taoist classic of the Way, tradition says by Lao-tzu

sage.meaning: a wise person; the book's model of how to live

uncarved wood.meaning: an earlier chapter's picture of plain, unshaped simplicity

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching 81 (true words aren't beautiful, beautiful words aren't true; the good don't argue; those who know aren't widely learned; the sage doesn't hoard, and the more he gives the more he has; heaven benefits and doesn't harm, the sage acts and doesn't contend)

notes: Chapter 81 is paraphrased; Legge's wording ('Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere') was not quoted because the writer could not confirm the whole passage word for word.

The teach calls this the final chapter and says the book closes on 'act and don't contend'; true of the received 81-chapter order. Some manuscripts order the chapters differently; confirm the path's framing.
Original 信言不美 (xìn yán bù měi) rendered 'SHIN yen boo MAY'; confirm.
'After eighty chapters of water, valleys, and uncarved wood' refers back to the path's own earlier days (like water, be the valley, plain silk, uncarved wood).
